Where it began

Muttiah Muralitharan was born in Kandy on 17 April 1972, the eldest of four boys. At nine he went to St Anthony's College in the town, and he started out bowling medium pace. When he was 14 his school coach, Sunil Fernando, suggested off-spin instead, and batters everywhere came to regret it. In his last two school seasons he took more than a hundred wickets, enough to be named the Bata Schoolboy Cricketer of the Year for 1990-91.

After school he joined Tamil Union and went to England with Sri Lanka A in 1991, where five games brought him no wickets at all. It was not a sign of things to come.

The player

His Test debut came against Australia at the Khettarama Stadium on 28 August 1992, when he was 20, and Craig McDermott was his first victim. Six years later at The Oval he took 16 for 220 in the match, bowling more than 54 overs in the second innings for 9 for 65, as Sri Lanka won a Test in England for the first time. He called it the highlight of his career. In December 2007, in front of his home crowd in Kandy, he bowled Paul Collingwood to become the leading wicket-taker in Test history.

In 133 Tests from 1992 to 2010 he took 800 wickets at 22.73, with a best of 9 for 51, 67 five-wicket innings and 22 ten-wicket Tests. By November 2026 nobody had taken more. He went into his final Test, against India in July 2010, eight short of 800, and took the last one, Pragyan Ojha, with the final ball he bowled.

What made him special

He was an off-spinner with an unusually supple wrist, which brought him turn on any surface, and alongside the stock ball he had a fast top-spinner and the doosra, which went the other way. He took ten wickets in a match against every other Test nation.

Batting was another matter, though a cheerful one. Usually at number 11, he liked to back away and swing, and his best was 67 against India at Kandy. He once ran himself out by leaving his crease to congratulate Kumar Sangakkara on a hundred while the ball was in play.

Away from the middle

In 2002 Wisden's statistical study of every Test ranked him the finest Test bowler of all time, and Wisden named him its Leading Cricketer in the World for both 2000 and 2006. In 2017 he became the first Sri Lankan inducted into the ICC Hall of Fame. A portrait of him hangs at Lord's, and the stadium at Pallekele was renamed after him. He later coached the bowlers at Sunrisers Hyderabad, champions of the Indian Premier League in 2016.

And finally

By the end of his career he held the record for the most ducks in international cricket, 59 of them. It seems only fair: he spent so many years sending batters back without a run that the game was entitled to return the favour once in a while.
